text: Cent #1264.
A penny struck in 1944 with no mint
mark, generally indicating the Philadelphia mint.
22 of the 10,000 Cents are dated 1944.
None is dated 1943,
the year pennies were struck in steel.
It is a Wheat Club year,
and a year of the 1940s Set,
which no Wall had completed
as of October 2026.
This Cent is the oldest Gold
Cent in the collection, by 12 years.
The Traits Atlas of the CENTS Trait Council
describes gold patina as a luminous surface
toning, suspended between metal and light.
This one is Notable Gold.
The other grade, Full, is a continuous golden
sheen over more than about
70 percent of the surface.
69 Cents carry gold.
Every other one was struck in 1956 or later.
Over Lincoln's head lies Significant Obsidian:
in the Atlas's words, a major visual actor
with strong darkening, but not yet fully dominant.
Near the rim, a fleck of paint
marks it as Contaminated.
Compare Cent #543,
also from 1944, with no visual trait.
The same design, the same year.
Only one of them turned gold.
Time-based generative art.
In the words of Martin Lehnen,
in his essay "Thoughts about the unique
nature of CENTS traits and their significance":
"Each CENT is a high-resolution photograph
of a genuine coin, and its traits are natural
phenomena like wear, patina,
and imperfections – etched by time, not code."
Years that carry meaning.
In the same essay: "…coins from significant
historical years become highly coveted,
adding a layer of historical
storytelling to the project."
Cent #1264, a great Cent.
